newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba takes tight-lipped approach to Lima drama.
newsitem.headline: Cuba takes tight-lipped approach to Lima drama.

text.p: Cuba, at the centre of speculation about a possible mediating role in the Lima hostage drama, is maintaining a deliberately discreet and low-key approach to the affair.
So far, President Fidel Castro's government has pointedly refrained from making any public judgment of the Lima events.

It has refused to comment on the possibility of mediation by communist-ruled Cuba to secure the release of the hostages held by leftist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Cuba has followed this situation with special attention from the very first moment and is keeping in permanent contact with the Peruvian authorities," the foreign ministry said in a brief public statement released on Friday.
Apart from confirming that the Cuban ambassador to Lima and another Cuban diplomat are among the hostages, Cuban government spokesmen have been very careful to avoid going beyond this position.

When pressed by journalists, they reply that Cuba would prefer not to indulge in speculation and that "silence has its value." Cuba's state media have limited themselves to reporting the drama with little sensation or comment.

The Lima hostage crisis, however, generated a flurry of diplomatic activity in Havana from Wednesday onwards. The ambassadors of Peru, Canada and Japan were among those diplomats who held several consultations with Cuba's Foreign Ministry or among themselves about the situation. Other embassies also showed a keen interest in Cuba's position.
There are several precedents fuelling speculation about a possible mediation role for Cuba, which has granted asylum to leftist guerrillas to help resolve similar crisis in the past.

Last June, Castro used his good offices to help secure the release of former Colombian President Cesar Gaviria's brother from a Colombian leftist group of kidnappers. Some of the kidnappers subsequently flew to Havana with their families as part of what Cuban officials called a "humanitarian solution".

The Lima hostage drama has also revived memories of a similar event in 1980, when Colombian M-19 guerrillas seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican embassy residence in Bogota to demand the release of more than 300 jailed colleagues.
The siege lasted for more than two months and ended without bloodshed when the guerrillas dropped their demands and freed their hostages after flying to Cuba in a plane sent by Castro.

Foreign diplomats said the Cuban government, which is very sensitive about its image in the post-Cold War world, apparently preferred to keep its options open by maintaining a discreet silence. At least one foreign ambassador in Havana had privately urged the government to condemn the MRTA guerrillas' armed seizure of the Japanese residence in Lima.
"The Cubans seem to take the view that whatever they say, it'll be a case of 'damned if we do and damned if we don't', so they prefer to keep their mouths shut," a senior diplomat said.

Since the break-up after 1991 of the former Soviet Union, Cuba's main political, military and economic ally for more than three decades, Castro has said publicly that Cuba is no longer supporting armed revolution in Latin America and is concentrating instead on its own survival and development.

Although the Peruvian MRTA guerrilla movement is reported to be inspired by the Cuban Revolution, Havana-based diplomats said they were not aware of any strong past or existing links with the Cuban government.
Given Cuba's determined, deliberate silence over the Lima drama, if any Cuban mediation or participation in a solution occurs, it is likely to come to light only after the event.
